UnitStatement: Architecture refers to structural component layout and to load-bearing decisions that determine enforceable system capabilities and limits.
The architecture chapter is organized around substrate, entity model, lifecycle, agent hierarchy, write scope, invariants, orchestration, and brief-output contracts.
Chirality architecture operationalizes the ontological, epistemological, praxiological, and axiological pillars established in Chapter 3.
Chirality architecture is built from the structural logic of its philosophical principles rather than applying those principles after design.
Chirality represents project state as an implicit graph encoded entirely in git-tracked files.
Filesystem-as-state is the load-bearing architectural decision on which every other architectural capability depends.
Architectural capabilities would not be preserved if project state migrated to an external system.
Project graph nodes are deliverable folders and package folders.
Each filesystem folder corresponds to an entity in the project domain.
Project graph edges are rows in Dependencies.csv registers.
Each dependency row encodes a directed relationship between a host deliverable and a target entity.
Dependency rows are classified as ANCHOR tree edges or EXECUTION directed acyclic graph edges.
ANCHOR and EXECUTION edge classes together form the project knowledge graph.
The ANCHOR tree preserves stable definitional intent.
The EXECUTION DAG captures execution-time couplings.
Project graph properties are plain markdown files inside each node folder.
_STATUS.md, _CONTEXT.md, _DEPENDENCIES.md, _REFERENCES.md, and the four-document kit carry deliverable identity, lifecycle state, traceability, and technical content.
The project graph has no representation other than the filesystem itself.
The architecture uses no translation layer, secondary index, or remote service for project graph state.
Agents, humans, and static analysis tools observe the same structure and parse the same files.
V-model traceability, immutable snapshots, change propagation tracking, content-addressed approval, and the audit trail depend on state being in git-tracked files.
Moving state to a database would require rebuilding each filesystem-dependent capability.
V-model traceability is achieved through ANCHOR-class dependency rows linking deliverables to scope items and objectives.
Traceability links in Dependencies.csv are stable, human-readable, and directly inspectable.
Database-backed traceability would require a separate schema and synchronization discipline.
Immutable snapshots are achieved through append-only history in timestamped directories.
A snapshot folder is never modified after creation.
Git history independently records when each snapshot was created and what it contained.
Change propagation tracking is computed by traversing the EXECUTION-class dependency graph encoded in Dependencies.csv files.
Every dependency potentially affected by an upstream change is identifiable without querying a service.
Git commit SHAs provide stable, unforgeable identifiers for versions of files.
Approvals recorded in versioned files bind to the SHA of the approved content.
If approved content changes, its SHA changes and the approval is voided under K-AUTH-2.
Git history serves as the audit trail without additional logging infrastructure.
Every agent write, human edit, and approval record is observable as a versioned commit.
The external-database framework comparison note is an editorial comparison prompt rather than a Chirality architecture requirement.
Notes: Bracketed COMPARE note, not a normative system statement.

UnitStatement: Forgoing an external database is primarily an auditability argument rather than a simplicity argument.
The forensic property of git history matches regulated-environment requirements for design record keeping.
The filesystem commitment enables offline operation without infrastructure dependencies.
The filesystem commitment enables agent execution by any compliant LLM runtime capable of reading and writing files.
The filesystem commitment enables human inspection of all state without specialized tooling.
The filesystem commitment enables direct integration with existing engineering document management workflows.
The filesystem commitment precludes external databases as sources of execution truth.
The filesystem commitment precludes server-side session state that diverges from on-disk content.
The filesystem commitment precludes hidden agent memory that persists across sessions outside versioned files.
The filesystem commitment precludes centralised dependency graphs that must be synchronized with deliverable-local registers.
The filesystem exclusions maintain the system auditability guarantees.
If information is not in a versioned file, it does not exist for purposes of reliance.
Capabilities requiring violation of the versioned-file reliance principle are outside the system scope by architectural definition.
The project hierarchy is deliberately flat: packages contain deliverables and there are no intermediate levels.
The hierarchy contains no phases, sub-packages, or task sub-levels within deliverables.
Invariant K-HIER-1 encodes the flat hierarchy constraint.
The flat hierarchy is enforced at the decomposition gate, during workspace scaffolding, and by human review of folder structures.
Each package represents a non-overlapping, gap-free partition of project scope.
Every scope item belongs to exactly one package.
Each deliverable belongs to exactly one package.
Each deliverable has a responsible party, a type classification, and one or more anticipated artifacts.
An artifact is any tangible output produced within a deliverable folder, including the standard four-document kit.
The flat hierarchy prioritizes automation reliability and coverage verifiability.
Nested hierarchies introduce ambiguity in scope assignment and make machine-checkable completeness proofs harder.
The flatness constraint enables the decomposition ledger to serve as a machine-checkable completeness artifact.
Identifiers are assigned once and persist across renames, path changes, and structural reorganization.
Path is a physical projection of decomposition rather than identity itself under K-ID-1.
Canonical identifier formats include PKG-XX for packages, DEL-XX-YY for deliverables, DEP-XX-YY-NNN for dependencies, SOW-NNN for scope items, and OBJ-NNN for objectives.
Deliverable IDs deterministically couple to package IDs by matching leading digits.
An agent can determine package membership from a deliverable ID alone without filesystem access.
Folder names combine the stable identifier with a human-readable filesystem-safe label.
_CONTEXT.md preserves the canonical unsanitized name within each deliverable folder.
SPEC.md defines the complete file inventory for a deliverable folder.
The PREPARATION agent creates the minimum viable fileset for a deliverable folder.
_STATUS.md records lifecycle state and history as the canonical lifecycle indicator under K-STATUS-1.
_CONTEXT.md records identity, decomposition pointer, and scope traceability.
_DEPENDENCIES.md records dependency summaries with human-declared and agent-extracted zones.
_REFERENCES.md records source document pointers.
_SEMANTIC.md begins as a semantic lens scaffold placeholder.
The full initialized state adds Datasheet.md, Specification.md, Guidance.md, and Procedure.md produced by TASK+four-documents.
Dependencies.csv, _MEMORY.md, and _SEMANTIC_LENSING.md are optional files added by subsequent agents as work proceeds.
TYPES.md establishes two classes of dependency relationships for the project knowledge graph.
ANCHOR-class edges are vertical tree edges connecting each deliverable upward to its definitional context.
Every deliverable carries exactly one IMPLEMENTS_NODE row linking it to its parent package or WBS node.
A deliverable carries zero or more TRACES_TO_REQUIREMENT rows linking it to scope items and objectives.
The ANCHOR tree is the traceability backbone for units of production.
EXECUTION-class edges are horizontal DAG edges capturing information flow and production dependencies between deliverables.
EXECUTION-class edges encode prerequisite, interface, handover, constraint, and enablement relationships.
The ANCHOR tree encodes static project topology established at decomposition time and rarely changed.
The EXECUTION DAG encodes dynamic production couplings that evolve as agents extract dependencies from deliverable content.
Together, the ANCHOR tree and EXECUTION DAG answer both requirements-traceability and production-dependency questions.
The deliverable lifecycle is a linear state machine with six states.
The deliverable lifecycle sequence is OPEN -> INITIALIZED -> SEMANTIC_READY -> IN_PROGRESS -> CHECKING -> ISSUED.
OPEN means PREPARATION has created the folder and minimum viable fileset, with no substantive content.
INITIALIZED means TASK+four-documents has generated the four-document kit.
SEMANTIC_READY means TASK+semantic-matrix-build has generated _SEMANTIC.md.
IN_PROGRESS means a human or WORKING_ITEMS agent has commenced active substantive work.
CHECKING means a human has moved the deliverable to the review staging area.
ISSUED means a human has approved the deliverable and released it for use.
The transition into OPEN is authorized only for PREPARATION.
The OPEN -> INITIALIZED transition is authorized only for TASK+four-documents.
The INITIALIZED -> SEMANTIC_READY transition is authorized only for TASK+semantic-matrix-build.
The INITIALIZED -> IN_PROGRESS transition is authorized for a human or WORKING_ITEMS when the semantic step is skipped.
The SEMANTIC_READY -> IN_PROGRESS transition is authorized for a human or WORKING_ITEMS.
The IN_PROGRESS -> CHECKING transition is authorized only for a human.
The CHECKING -> ISSUED transition is authorized only for a human.
Forward transitions through OPEN, INITIALIZED, and SEMANTIC_READY are agent-authorized confirmations of completed mechanical preparation.
Forward transitions through CHECKING and ISSUED are human-only consequential transitions.
No agent type can move deliverables to external review or release work for reliance.
The INITIALIZED -> SEMANTIC_READY transition is optional.
If semantic lensing is omitted, deliverables may transition directly from INITIALIZED to IN_PROGRESS.
Semantic enrichment is available when it adds value, but its absence does not block production.
Lifecycle states track the production status of individual deliverables and are recorded in _STATUS.md.
Stage gates are human-managed checkpoints representing aggregate progress targets across deliverables.
Stage gates are not lifecycle states and are tracked separately in coordination records.
_STATUS.md answers whether an individual deliverable is ready for review.
Project stage-gate status requires aggregation across the project by SCHEDULING and RECONCILIATION agents.
K-STATUS-1 makes _STATUS.md the canonical human-readable lifecycle state file for each deliverable.
No file other than _STATUS.md determines deliverable lifecycle state.
Before a lifecycle-relevant write, an agent must read _STATUS.md to determine operation validity.
Attempting to initialize a deliverable already in IN_PROGRESS is a precondition failure.
K-STATUS-1 enforcement appears in every lifecycle-sensitive agent SPEC and in ORCHESTRATOR context sealing.
The warrant lifecycle tracks the epistemic state of claims within a deliverable.
The six epistemic primitives are claim, warrant, status, gap, conflict, and ruling.
The warrant lifecycle sequence is UNWARRANTED -> CITED -> REVIEWED -> AUTHENTICATED.
A deliverable in IN_PROGRESS may contain claims in varying warrant states.
The transition to CHECKING requires critical claims to have been warranted.
The transition to ISSUED requires professional authentication that the aggregate warrant state is sufficient for reliance.
The agent system is organized into three types with strictly partitioned responsibilities.
The agent type hierarchy enforces the system authority model.
Type 0 agents define invariant protocols and design standards that downstream agents must conform to.
Type 0 agents do not write project state.
The Type 0 layer is the constitutional layer of the system.
The Type 0 layer consists of HELPS_HUMANS and DECOMP_BASE.
Agent instructions that disagree with Type 0 standards must be edited to conform to the standards.
Type 1 agents are human-facing orchestrators for conversational, gate-controlled workflows.
Type 1 agents may spawn Type 2 agents.
Type 1 agents own orchestration decisions but do not own engineering content.
Type 2 agents are brief-driven specialists operating in straight-through execution mode.
Type 2 agents receive structured inputs, produce auditable outputs, and return to their invoking agent without mid-run human interaction.
Type 2 agents never spawn other agents.
The multi-agent framework comparison note is an editorial comparison prompt rather than a Chirality authority requirement.
Notes: Bracketed COMPARE note, not a normative system statement.

UnitStatement: Type 2 specialists cannot escalate to Type 1 authority.
Type 2 agents cannot initiate gate reviews, spawn other agents, or make scope decisions.
A Type 2 agent encountering a scope question must record it as TBD and surface it in the run report.
Type 1 managers cannot override Type 0 constraints.
An orchestration decision requiring violation of a Type 0 constraint is not valid.
Human gates cannot be bypassed by any agent type.
No agent can approve deliverables for external reliance, resolve conflicts authoritatively, commit to the baseline, or advance lifecycle to CHECKING or ISSUED.
Each agent instruction file declares six properties in a standardized header block.
AGENT_TYPE declares the agent position in the hierarchy.
AGENT_CLASS declares whether the agent uses a conversational persona interface or straight-through task execution.
INTERACTION_SURFACE declares how the agent is invoked.
WRITE_SCOPE declares what filesystem area the agent may write to.
BLOCKING declares whether an agent may pause for human input.
PRIMARY_OUTPUTS declares what the agent produces.
Agent header properties are enforceable constraints rather than metadata.
BLOCKING: never on Type 2 agents means no mid-run human decision is required or possible.
A Type 2 agent encountering ambiguity must record it as TBD rather than pause the run.
WRITE_SCOPE determines exactly which filesystem zones an agent may touch.
The write scope model enforces formal separation between source truth and derived outputs.
Every agent is assigned to exactly one write-scope category.
An agent write outside its declared scope is an architectural violation of K-WRITE-1.
NONE is a read-only write scope in which the agent may draft content but may not write anywhere.
The NONE write scope applies to HELPS_HUMANS, DECOMP_BASE, and HELP_HUMAN.
REPO-METADATA-ONLY agents may write instruction files, README files, and templates but not execution truth.
The REPO-METADATA-ONLY write scope applies to DOMAIN_DECOMP and CONTEXT_TRANSPOSE.
PROJECT-LEVEL agents may write decomposition documents, project metadata files, and folder scaffolding.
The PROJECT-LEVEL write scope applies to PROJECT_DECOMP, SOFTWARE_DECOMP, SCOPE_CHANGE, PREPARATION, and ESTIMATE_PREP.
DELIVERABLE-LOCAL agents may write only within a single assigned production unit folder.
The DELIVERABLE-LOCAL write scope applies to WORKING_ITEMS, TASK variants, DELIVERABLE_TASK, and REVIEW.
TOOL-ROOT-ONLY agents may write only to a specific designated tool root under EXECUTION_ROOT.
The TOOL-ROOT-ONLY write scope applies to orchestration, reconciliation, change, scheduling, estimating, aggregation, audit, hypergraph, and evaluation outputs.
DBM presents write-scope assignments in a tree format.
WORKING_ITEMS is deliverable-local with a standing exception for NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md.
TASK+dependency-extract is deliverable-local for dependency artifacts only.
REVIEW is deliverable-local with a tool-root exception for snapshots.
The write scope tree includes a REPO-WIDE scope for TOOLMAKER and SKILLMAKER.
Notes: Section 4.6.1 says there are five scope categories, but the tree adds REPO-WIDE.

UnitStatement: ORCHESTRATOR writes to _Coordination under TOOL-ROOT-ONLY scope.
RECONCILIATION writes to _Reconciliation under TOOL-ROOT-ONLY scope.
CHANGE writes to _Change and approved repository files under TOOL-ROOT-ONLY scope with an approval gate.
DOMAIN_HYPERGRAPH writes to _Aggregation/Hypergraph under TOOL-ROOT-ONLY scope.
EVALUATION and its subordinate report agents write under _Evaluation tool roots.
Every agent declares its write scope in the Agent Header Block.
Deliverable-local agents cannot write outside their assigned production unit folder.
Tool-root agents write only to their designated tool root under EXECUTION_ROOT.
Tool-root agents never modify source truth in deliverable production documents.
_STATUS.md updates are restricted to designated agents and only for forward lifecycle transitions.
WORKING_ITEMS sessions prohibit cross-deliverable scanning or editing unless a human explicitly requests a cross-check.
Write scope provides fault containment by limiting failures to the zone an agent can write.
A Type 2 task-agent failure can corrupt only the zone to which that agent has write access.
Tool-root agents cannot write source truth, and deliverable-local agents cannot write other deliverables.
Write quarantine establishes formal fault containment zones through structural impossibility of cross-zone writes.
A monitoring approach detects violations after occurrence, whereas the write scope model prevents cross-zone violations from being representable.
A Type 2 agent under WORKING_ITEMS attempting to modify another deliverable is outside its declared scope.
The broad-tool-access framework comparison note is an editorial comparison prompt rather than a Chirality write-scope requirement.
Notes: Bracketed COMPARE note, not a normative system statement.

UnitStatement: Declaring write scope at the agent level makes the scope contract visible and auditable in the instruction file.
Agent-level write scope can express project-domain semantics that generic operating-system permissions cannot express.
Chirality maintains agent behavior through three complementary contract layers defined in DBM Section 4.
R1-R9 workflow design requirements apply to all agents and to new agent workflow designs.

R1-R9 require explicit human decision rights, straight-through task agents, write quarantine, immutable snapshots, mandatory provenance, no-invention behavior, surfaced conflicts, brief-driven execution, and hygienic publication.
I1-I10 decomposition invariants apply to PROJECT_DECOMP, SOFTWARE_DECOMP, and DOMAIN_DECOMP.
AUDIT_DECOMP verifies the I1-I10 decomposition invariants.

I1-I10 govern human-validated gates, no-invention scope assignment, flat partitions, no overlaps or gaps, stable identifiers, deterministic ID coupling, objective mapping, rationale, ledger telemetry, and vocabulary discipline.
The K-* catalog defines system-wide binding constraints.
PROJECT_DECOMP and PREPARATION primarily enforce K-HIER-1 and K-ID-1 for hierarchy and identity.
REVIEW and CHANGE approval gates primarily enforce K-AUTH-1, K-AUTH-2, and K-BIND-1 for authority and approval.
ORCHESTRATOR and Type 2 agents primarily enforce K-SEAL-1 and K-GHOST-1 for sealing and context.
TASK+dependency-extract and AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE primarily enforce K-DEP-1 and K-DEP-2 for dependencies.
PREPARATION, TASK+four-documents, TASK+semantic-matrix-build, and REVIEW primarily enforce K-STATUS-1 for status.
AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE and RECONCILIATION primarily enforce K-STALE-1, K-STALE-2, and K-VAL-1 for staleness and validation.
ORCHESTRATOR and SCHEDULING primarily enforce K-GATE-1 for gates.
CHANGE primarily enforces K-MERGE-1 for merge behavior.
TASK+dependency-extract primarily enforces K-PROV-1 by requiring evidence citations on every row.
All agents enforce K-INVENT-1 for invention control.
All agents enforce K-CONFLICT-1 for conflict handling.
All agents enforce K-WRITE-1 for write scope.
All snapshot-producing agents enforce K-SNAP-1 for snapshots.
K-* invariants are distributed across four enforcement layers at different points of system operation.
Design-time enforcement constrains agent behavior through the content of agent instruction files before runtime invocation.
K-GHOST-1, K-WRITE-1, K-SNAP-1, K-PROV-1, K-INVENT-1, K-CONFLICT-1, K-DEP-1, and K-DEP-2 are enforced at design time.
ORCHESTRATOR enforces K-SEAL-1, K-GATE-1, and K-HIER-1 at runtime during active session management.
ORCHESTRATOR checks sealed context, gate approval, and gate-map conformity before dispatching Type 2 agents.
Human review at defined gates enforces binding approvals, staleness triage, merge authorization, and consequential lifecycle state management.
K-AUTH-1, K-AUTH-2, K-BIND-1, K-STALE-2, K-MERGE-1, K-VAL-1, and K-STATUS-1 are enforced through human gates.
K-STALE-1, K-VAL-1, K-MERGE-1, K-AUTH-2, and K-DEP-2 are candidates for future automated tooling.
Future tooling is expected to cover SHA comparison, staleness computation, and dependency resolution validation.
Distributed enforcement prevents any single failure mode from violating all constraints simultaneously.
Instruction-level constraints are intended to prevent agents from describing conforming execution paths that violate invariants.
Instruction-level enforcement depends on instruction quality maintained by Type 0 canonical standards and AUDIT_AGENTS.
The spawning graph defines which agents may initiate which other agents.
HELP_HUMAN classifies intent and routes but does not spawn other agents.
ORCHESTRATOR may spawn PREPARATION, TASK variants, DOMAIN_HYPERGRAPH, ESTIMATING, and AGGREGATION.
WORKING_ITEMS may spawn TASK.
RECONCILIATION may spawn dependency, agent, decomposition, epistemic, governance, scope-closure, and hypergraph-closure audit agents.
EVALUATION may spawn CONTENT_DIGEST, EVALUATION_REPORT, EVALUATION_STRUCTURE_AUDIT, and EVALUATION_DEPENDENCY_AUDIT.
CHANGE is a leaf agent that implements approved edits and spawns nothing.
TOOLMAKER and SKILLMAKER are standalone agents.
REVIEW triggers AUDIT_DECOMP as a precondition check.
SCOPE_CHANGE hands off to ORCHESTRATOR and CHANGE.
CONTEXT_TRANSPOSE hands off to CHANGE for publication.
SCHEDULING is standalone, reads the dependency graph, and produces schedule artifacts.
The spawning graph is acyclic by construction.
No Type 2 agent spawns any other agent.
Spawning Type 1 agents do not spawn each other.
Acyclic spawning bounds execution-tree depth and prevents runaway spawning cascades.
ORCHESTRATOR maintains session continuity through NEXT_INSTANCE_PROMPT.md and NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md.
NEXT_INSTANCE_PROMPT.md is stable, updated only on protocol changes, and contains session startup instructions.
NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md is mutable at each handoff and contains pointers, program state, active rulings, and immediate next actions.
ORCHESTRATOR creates the session handoff files during workspace initialization.
WORKING_ITEMS reads the session handoff files at the start of each session.
WORKING_ITEMS updates NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md at session end.
CHANGE verifies NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md before committing.
Session handoff externalizes program state to versioned files instead of relying on LLM context memory.
A future session that reads the handoff files acquires the same program state as a continuous session.
The session-continuity guarantee is a property of the filesystem rather than the language model.
The operational control loop begins with ORCHESTRATOR initializing workspace and session handoff artifacts while managing gates.
WORKING_ITEMS reads session state and executes deliverable-level work through pre-authorized TASK dispatches.
TASK+dependency-extract reruns after content changes to keep dependency registers current.
RECONCILIATION aggregates and audits across the project through closure reports and coverage analyses.
CHANGE applies approved commit instructions and requires explicit approval tokens before state-changing actions.
The control loop returns to WORKING_ITEMS with updated state in NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md.
The control loop is human-triggered at each session rather than continuous.
The architecture does not run agents autonomously between human interactions.
Each session starts when a human opens the workbench and ends when they commit and close.
DBM defines four spawning mechanisms with distinct authorization requirements.
ORCHESTRATOR uses human-gated phases requiring explicit human confirmation at each sequential phase.
WORKING_ITEMS uses pre-authorized dispatch after the human confirms the session objective once.
RECONCILIATION uses a human-directed toolbelt in which the human provides the authorized agent list.
RECONCILIATION runs one task per cycle by default under the human-directed toolbelt mechanism.
CHANGE uses approval-gated execution requiring APPROVE or APPROVE_DESTRUCTIVE tokens per action.
Per-action authorization overhead is reduced deliberately as consequence level and repetition patterns change.
ORCHESTRATOR phases are high-stakes and infrequent, while WORKING_ITEMS task dispatch is routine and repetitive.
CHANGE has the most stringent authorization requirement because it modifies repository state.
The agent-framework authorization comparison note is an editorial comparison prompt rather than a Chirality spawning requirement.

UnitStatement: The INIT-TASK brief is the standard input contract for all Type 2 agents.
An INIT-TASK brief is a structured parameter table rather than natural language.
INIT-TASK input may be supplied inline or through an INIT-TASK.md file, with inline fields taking precedence.
The INIT-TASK base template includes PURPOSE, SCOPE, WHERE_TO_LOOK, OUTPUT_LABEL, CONFIG, CONSTRAINTS, EXCLUSIONS, and NOTES.
Individual agents extend the INIT-TASK base template with domain-specific parameters.
TASK+dependency-extract extends INIT-TASK with MODE, STRICTNESS, and SOURCE_DOCS parameters.
TASK+four-documents extends INIT-TASK with RUN_PASSES, ALLOW_OVERWRITE_STATES, and DECOMP_VARIANT parameters.
The INIT-TASK brief makes agent inputs deterministic and repeatable.
Identical briefs on identical filesystem state should produce equivalent outputs.
The INIT-TASK brief enables pre-flight validation and FAILED_INPUTS halting for incomplete or structurally invalid briefs.
The INIT-TASK brief creates an auditable record by being written verbatim into snapshot Brief.md files.
DBM defines a standard output convention for agents that produce analysis outputs to tool roots.
Agent snapshots are stored under TOOL_ROOT using agent prefix, run label, date, and time components.
A standard snapshot contains Brief.md, RUN_SUMMARY.md, QA_Report.md, Decision_Log.md, agent-specific outputs, and optional Evidence.
_LATEST.md is a mutable pointer to the most recent snapshot under a tool root.
Readers use _LATEST.md to find current tool-root state and use chronological snapshot folders to inspect history.
K-SNAP-1 states that task-agent outputs to tool roots are immutable snapshots.
K-SNAP-1 permits pointer files to be overwritten but forbids modifying snapshot folders.
Immutable snapshots preserve an unambiguous relationship between a git commit and the run that produced the snapshot.
The immutability rule makes git history a faithful record of committed snapshots.
Committed immutable snapshots make the snapshot trail equivalent to a regulated-environment audit trail.
Reruns produce new snapshots without modifying existing snapshots.
A rerun result is additional evidence rather than a replacement for the previous result.
Human review of the diff between snapshots is sufficient to judge whether a rerun resolved issues or introduced findings.
Chirality architecture is a structure-as-governance system.
Chirality capabilities arise from structural constraints rather than the sophistication of individual agents.
Filesystem-as-state operationalizes the ontological pillar by making the domain model inspectable and version-controllable.
Evidence-first design operationalizes the epistemological pillar by making claim reliability structurally visible.
Agent type hierarchy and write scope architecture operationalize the praxiological pillar by bounding authority, containing failures, and structuralizing human gates.
Invariant systems and non-bypassable human lifecycle gates operationalize professional responsibility as architectural constraints.
The architecture prevents agents from approving deliverables, escaping write zones, or hiding epistemic output status.
